title: Develop and implement a food safety and quality management system in an agricultural supply chain

lessons.title: Food safety hazards and management systems
lessons.html:
Why food safety systems?

Food produced on farms reaches consumers through packhouses, abattoirs, processors and retailers. A single contamination incident can cause illness, deaths, recalls, lost markets and legal action. South Africa's 2017-2018 listeriosis outbreak, linked to processed meat, showed how serious failures can be. Buyers, retailers and export markets therefore require documented food safety and quality management systems.

Types of hazards

HazardExamples
BiologicalSalmonella, E. coli, Listeria, parasites, viruses from manure, water, workers, pests
ChemicalPesticide and veterinary drug residues, cleaning chemicals, mycotoxins, heavy metals
PhysicalGlass, metal, stones, wood, jewellery
AllergensRelevant in processing: nuts, milk, egg, wheat and others

Food safety versus quality

Safety means the food will not harm the consumer. Quality means it meets the specifications the customer expects: size, colour, taste, shelf life. A management system covers both, but safety always comes first.

Common systems and standards

  • Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) at farm level, often certified through GLOBALG.A.P. for export and retail.
  • HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) for processing and packing.
  • ISO 22000 and FSSC 22000 as full food safety management systems.
  • Retailer-specific audit schemes.

South African law also applies: the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 and its regulations (including those on hygiene requirements for food premises), the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 for abattoirs, and Act 36 of 1947 for registered remedies and their use.

lessons.title: Developing the system: prerequisites and HACCP
lessons.html:
Building the foundation

Prerequisite programmes (PRPs)

HACCP works only on top of basic good practices:

  • Personal hygiene and health of workers; toilets and hand-washing near fields and packhouses.
  • Cleaning and sanitation schedules.
  • Water quality testing for irrigation, washing and processing.
  • Pest control programme.
  • Safe storage and use of chemicals.
  • Supplier approval for inputs and packaging.
  • Maintenance and calibration of equipment.
  • Waste management.
  • Training of all staff.
  • Traceability and recall procedures.

The seven HACCP principles

  1. Conduct a hazard analysis for every step in the process flow.
  2. Determine critical control points (CCPs): steps where control is essential to prevent or eliminate a hazard.
  3. Establish critical limits for each CCP (e.g. a minimum chlorine concentration in wash water, or a cooking temperature).
  4. Establish monitoring procedures.
  5. Establish corrective actions when monitoring shows a limit is not met.
  6. Establish verification procedures to confirm the system works.
  7. Establish documentation and record keeping.

Preliminary steps

Form a multidisciplinary HACCP team, describe the product and its intended use, draw a process flow diagram and verify it on the floor before starting the hazard analysis.

Example: a packhouse for fresh vegetables

Steps: receiving, washing, sorting, packing, cooling, dispatch. Hazards include microbes in wash water and residues from the field. Controls might be wash water sanitiser concentration (monitored and recorded), supplier spray records checked at receiving, and cold-chain temperature at dispatch. Whether a step is a CCP depends on the hazard analysis for that specific operation.

lessons.title: Implementing, verifying and improving the system
lessons.html:
Making the system work every day

Implementation

  • Management commitment: a food safety policy signed by management, with resources.
  • Documentation: procedures, work instructions and record forms written simply, in the languages workers use.
  • Training: induction and refresher training for all staff, with records.
  • Responsibilities: named people for monitoring CCPs and PRPs.

Traceability

Every batch must be traceable one step back (supplier, field, block, animal) and one step forward (customer). Use batch or lot codes on packaging and records linking harvest, packing and dispatch. Test the system with mock recalls: can you trace a batch within hours?

Verification and auditing

  • Internal audits against the standard, at planned intervals.
  • Review of monitoring records and corrective actions by a supervisor.
  • Laboratory testing of products, water and surfaces.
  • External certification audits.

Corrective action and continual improvement

When something goes wrong (a failed residue test, a customer complaint, a foreign object), find the root cause, correct it, and prevent recurrence. Hold product that may be unsafe until a decision is made. Review the whole system at least annually and whenever processes, products or regulations change.

Food safety culture

Systems fail when people see them as paperwork. Encourage workers to report problems without fear, recognise good practice and make supervisors role models.

Key points

  • Hazards are biological, chemical, physical and allergens.
  • Prerequisite programmes are the foundation for HACCP.
  • HACCP has seven principles from hazard analysis to record keeping.
  • Traceability one step back and forward must be tested with mock recalls.
  • Verify through audits and testing, correct root causes and build a food safety culture.
